props.title: Twister
props.initialSlug: Storm chasers risk it all to study killer tornadoes

sections.content: Twister revolutionized disaster films with groundbreaking CGI tornadoes and launched a wave of 90s natural disaster blockbusters. Director Jan de Bont, fresh off Speed (1994), delivered intense practical effects mixed with early computer graphics that hold up surprisingly well. The film's influence echoes through later weather-focused disasters like The Day After Tomorrow (2004) and Into the Storm (2014). Helen Hunt and Bill Paxton's electric chemistry as storm-chasing researchers grounded the spectacle in human drama, while the innovative "Dorothy" research device became iconic.

sections.content: The mid-90s marked peak practical effects meeting emerging CGI capabilities. Twister's flying cows and tornado sequences required Industrial Light & Magic to develop new particle systems and air flow simulations. This technical breakthrough paved the way for Independence Day (1996) and Volcano (1997), establishing the template for modern disaster films. The film's attention to storm chasing authenticity, despite some Hollywood embellishments, sparked public interest in tornado research and meteorology.

Beyond its technical achievements, Twister exemplifies the disaster genre's shift from pure destruction porn to character-driven narratives. Like Deep Impact (1998) and Armageddon (1998), it balances spectacular devastation with personal stakes. The film's success influenced disaster movies to focus on scientists and researchers rather than just victims, seen later in 2012 (2009) and Greenland (2020). sections.content: Twister's DNA appears throughout modern weather-focused thrillers. Crawl (2019) borrows its intimate approach to natural threats, while Moonfall (2022) echoes its scientist-heroes-save-the-day structure. The film's practical effects philosophy influenced Christopher Nolan's approach to Interstellar (2014), where real tornado footage was incorporated into science fiction scenarios.
